summary: You send a prompt, stare at a blank screen, and then the whole answer drops at once. The AI apps you use every day avoid that by streaming the answer word by word, and you can build the same thing into your own agents. Why AI apps show their answers word by word, and how to build that into your own agents. A language model already generates its answer one token at a time, each token predicted from everything before it. Streaming just sends each token the moment it's generated instead of waiting for the whole response. The model isn't any faster, but time to first token (TTFT) drops, so the app feels much quicker. Under the hood, the connection between your app and the server stays open, and the server pushes each token through it as it's produced, usually over HTTP streaming or Server-Sent Events (SSE). summary: Pasting the same error back and saying "still broken, try again" gives your agent nothing new, so it starts guessing. Give it what you expected, what actually happened, and the full error, and it has somewhere to start. Vibe coding is great until the errors start piling up. You paste the error in, ask for a fix, it doesn't work, you say "try again," and the agent keeps guessing because you haven't given it anything new. Sometimes it rewrites the whole file, sometimes it fixes the original bug and quietly creates a new one. The fix starts with better information. Tell the agent what you expected and what happened instead (you clicked save, the button spun, the request returned a 500, nothing was saved), and include the whole error message and stack trace even if you don't understand every line. For visual bugs, attach a screenshot. Before it changes any code, talk the problem through with it first. Adding "don't change anything yet" keeps an enthusiastic agent from rewriting things while you test one idea at a time. Follow AWS Developers! summary: Automated reasoning uses logic to check whether a precise rule holds for every behaviour covered by a model. This 101-level explainer shows how it can answer questions you could never test exhaustively, and where the proof stops. I use one fictional online shop all the way through: an AI support agent, customer records in Amazon S3, and a database that should never be reachable from the internet. The same question follows each part of the system: what must never happen? A four-line loop shows how automated reasoning differs from testing. Then a real Verus specification shows the harder problem: a formal verification result can be valid even when you asked the checker to prove the wrong rule. From there, I look at how AWS uses automated reasoning in IAM Access Analyzer and VPC Reachability Analyzer. A checker can return a proof, a counterexample, or Unknown. An LLM can help write the rule, but it cannot decide what you meant. The refund example makes that painfully clear: two $300 refunds can slip through a rule that only checks whether each refund exceeds $500. Every result has a boundary. You need to know what property was stated, what was modelled, what was assumed, and what sat outside the model. Read Amazon Science's story about a decade of the Automated Reasoning Group: https://go.aws/4kMdkrG Follow AWS Developers! summary: Every mock is a guess about how an AWS service behaves. In this video I show what happens when the guess is wrong, and how to catch it on your own computer and in CI. The sample app is a small pub game on Amazon SQS and Amazon DynamoDB. Customers order, the bartender serves, and the order is deleted from the queue. I start with mocks. An agent writes a fake SQS and a fake DynamoDB, and the tests pass on my machine and in GitHub Actions. One of them should have failed. The fake builds the receipt handle from the message ID. The real SQS gives you a new receipt handle every time you receive the same message. The test is a false positive, and I hit this exact bug in a real project. Then I run the same test against real AWS, which takes about 25 seconds and needs an account with credentials. After that I run it against AWS Emulator, a local emulator for AWS APIs for development and testing. The emulator run takes about a fifth of the time, the CI job finishes in 56 seconds, and the state stays on my machine. Mocks stay for my own logic and for errors I want on demand. The emulator takes over when the test depends on how the service behaves. The cloud is for what the emulator does not cover yet. AWS Emulator does not check IAM policies, so it is not for security testing. summary: Set up Claude Code with the AWS MCP Server and AWS skills from the Agent Toolkit for AWS, then watch one of those skills keep a secret out of your agent’s chat. The aws-core plugin gives Claude Code the AWS MCP Server (current AWS docs, plus AWS API calls logged in CloudTrail) and tested skills the agent loads only when a task needs one. It also adds a hook that blocks direct secret fetches. Ask a coding agent for a secret and it fetches it the obvious way, so the plaintext lands in the model’s context and in your session files on disk. With the plugin, the same prompt gets refused, and the agent uses the secret through asm-exec without ever seeing it. I ran 10 tests for the blog: the hook blocked every secret fetch, including a boto3 call buried in a Python script, and let normal commands through. It’s a best-effort defense, not a security boundary, so keep least-privilege IAM underneath.
